content:
The crisp autumn air, hinting at the imminent arrival of winter, carried the faint, sweet scent of melted chocolate. It was countdown season, a time when supermarket shelves groaned under the weight of advent calendars of all shapes and sizes. The traditional chocolate-based variety remained king, of course, despite the contemporary trend of expanding into more… *adult* territory. Cosmetics, miniature bottles of gin, and even artisanal cheeses were vying for a place on the festive mantelpiece. However, the promise of a small square of milk chocolate daily, the anticipation building towards Christmas day, still held a unique, irresistible charm.

***

My gaze drifted down the glistening aisle, passing the glitzy boxes adorned with Disney characters and winter wonderlands. Affiliate links, I knew, were cunningly embedded within many of these enticing displays, designed to lure me – and, quite possibly, other Guardian readers – into impulsive purchases. The journalist had mentioned a “small commission” that may be earned, a subtle reminder that the news outlet's coverage, as independent as it strives to be, is occasionally tethered to the commercial world. I made a mental note to avoid the elaborately packaged options, gravitating toward the less flashy, more straightforward calendars.

***

My own Advent calendar traditions had evolved over the years. As a child, it was always the thrill of the foil-covered chocolate and the tiny Christmas themed image behind the door. Now, the anticipation extended beyond the treats themselves. It was now a daily dose of mindfulness, a way to savor small moments in an otherwise hectic season. My daughter had grown to this ritual with the same zeal, so the next mission was to get the best calendar. It would have to be simple, not overly sugary, and preferably, ethically sourced.

***

The choice was overwhelming. Chocolate brands battled for my attention, promising silky smooth textures and complex flavor profiles. Then there were the non-chocolate options: tea calendars, coffee calendars, even calendars featuring miniature bath bombs. The temptation was strong, not just to purchase for my daughter, but for myself as well. I paused, remembering the reminder about independent journalism. I had to make my own educated choice, carefully considering the products offered, setting aside the allure of the links.

***

Finally, after much deliberation, I settled on two calendars: one for my daughter and one for myself. Each was a classic: straightforward chocolate calendars with simple, iconic designs. As I brought the calendars to the till, I felt a sense of satisfaction, knowing I'd resisted the lure of the affiliate links and chosen something that brought simple joy. The anticipation of opening the first door, and the shared pleasure of the daily ritual would be all the reward needed. The Guardian’s disclaimer may have been present, but the true spirit of Christmas - independent joy and a shared moment - remained as strong as ever.
